Key: NH3 is one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms
Wrong choices (3N+3H, 3N+1H, 1N+1H) are all wrong for NH3
Context: a subscript counts the atoms of the symbol before it; no number means one atom

Context: cobalt is a hard, bluish-grey metal
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a hard, lustrous, bluish-gray transition metal'.

Wrong choices: carbon and oxygen joined or mixed would be written CO/CO2 (two capitals), not Co

Glucose is blood sugar, carried by the bloodstream to tissues and used by cells for energy
checks.note: Grokipedia confirms 'blood sugar' and fuel for ATP; Wikipedia confirms transport via the bloodstream.

checks.claim: Key: C6H12O6 holds twelve hydrogen atoms
checks.note: OpenStax: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, 6 oxygen.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: six (carbon/oxygen count), one, twenty-four (total atoms 6+12+6) are wrong
Context: plants make glucose by photosynthesis
Quartz is the mineral most sand is made of
checks.note: Grokipedia: sand grains 'predominantly consist of quartz (SiO2)'; tropical carbonate sands are the exception, which 'most' allows.

checks.claim: Quartz has the formula SiO2, a 3-D framework of SiO4 tetrahedra with each oxygen bridging two silicon atoms
Key: the formula of a network solid gives a ratio, two oxygen for every silicon
checks.note: Wikipedia: network solids have 'no individual molecules'; quartz is the example; formulas are ratios like ionic ones.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: 2 Si per O, 1 Si + 2 O in all, equal Si and O are all wrong
Stem: 'Each grain of quartz sand is a crystal'; context: 'the atoms link into one network through the whole grain'
checks.note: Many quartz sand grains are single crystals (monocrystalline), but a sizeable share are polycrystalline: aggregates of several crystals (studies of Holocene sands find 13-53% of quartz polycrystalline, depending on source rock). So not every grain is 'a crystal' with one network through it. Minor; fix: 'Each grain of quartz sand is made of crystal: silicon and oxygen atoms linked together' and in the context 'the atoms link into one network through the whole crystal'.

checks.claim: Oxygen in air is O2, colourless and odourless
Ozone O3 is a pale blue gas with a pungent smell that harms the lungs (respiratory irritant)
Key: O2 and O3 are two forms (allotropes) of one element
checks.note: Grokipedia names dioxygen and ozone as the example of allotropy.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: element and compound / two different elements / two different compounds are wrong (both hold only oxygen atoms)
checks.note: OpenStax: two-atom molecules of H, O, N are still elements.

checks.claim: Context: the ozone layer absorbs nearly all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light
checks.note: Grokipedia's wording ('nearly all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, including all UV-C and most UV-B'). Wikipedia notes most UV-A passes and is less harmful but not harmless; optional tightening: 'nearly all of the Sun's most harmful ultraviolet light'.

checks.claim: Key: a water molecule (one O joined to two H, three atoms) is the smallest particle that is still water
Wrong choices: no 'atom of water' exists; a lone oxygen atom is not water; a tiny droplet still holds many molecules
Context: 'A molecule is the smallest particle of a compound that keeps its makeup and properties'
checks.note: The source definition is 'retains its composition and CHEMICAL properties'. One water molecule has none of water's physical properties (wetness, boiling point, being a liquid): those belong to many molecules together, the same point the unit's Dalton question makes about a gold atom's shine. Dropping 'chemical' teaches the bulk-property misconception. Fix: 'keeps its makeup and chemical properties'.

checks.note: 'pale yellow-green', 'highly toxic as a pulmonary irritant'.

Context: table salt is safe to eat in moderation and needed by the body

checks.note: Wikipedia (Hofmann voltameter): 'This value is 2:1 experimentally.' 'Always' is fine at grade level; real tubes read close to, not exactly, 2:1.

checks.claim: Key: water holds two hydrogen atoms per oxygen atom; with both gases diatomic and equal volumes holding equal numbers of molecules, that gives 2:1 by volume
checks.note: Wikipedia notes the 2:1 matches H2O only if both gases are diatomic; the context says so, and gives Avogadro's equal-volumes rule (Grokipedia Gay-Lussac's law).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a hydrogen atom is not twice as big as an oxygen atom
checks.note: H vs O: empirical 25 vs 60 pm; van der Waals 110-120 vs 152; covalent 32 vs 63; calculated 53 vs 48. 'Nowhere near twice' holds on every measure.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: hydrogen gas is not twice as heavy as oxygen; hydrogen is the lightest element
Wrong choice: the same current flows through both electrodes (series circuit)
Joseph Proust was a French chemist
Key: Proust made artificial copper carbonate, compared it with natural copper carbonate, and found the same proportions by mass
checks.note: Grokipedia: copper carbonate 'from diverse natural and synthetic sources', fixed ratio about 5:1:4 Cu:C:O.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: more copper in his sample / varied with heat / changed batch to batch are all contrary to his finding
Context: Claude Berthollet, a French chemist, argued elements could combine in any proportions
checks.note: Essai de Statique Chimique, 1803; Wikipedia calls him 'Proust's fellow Frenchman' (born in Savoy, worked in France).

checks.claim: Context: the debate lasted years and was settled for Proust in the 1810s
checks.note: 'largely resolved in Proust's favor during the 1810s'; Wikipedia (Proust) dates acceptance to Berzelius in 1812 (citation needed).

checks.claim: Context: some crystals vary slightly and are called berthollides after Berthollet
checks.note: Kurnakov named berthollides after Berthollet; non-stoichiometric compounds are almost always solid inorganic compounds whose composition varies over a narrow range (wustite Fe0.95O). Strictly, berthollides are Kurnakov's sub-class of non-stoichiometric compounds; Grokipedia treats the names as synonyms, fine at grade level.

checks.claim: Water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom
Key: two H joined to two O is hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, a different compound
Context: pure H2O2 is a pale blue, syrupy (viscous) liquid and a strong bleach/oxidizer
checks.note: 'pale blue, viscous liquid', 'a powerful oxidizing agent', 'bleaching and cleaning agent'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: not water with an extra oxygen, not a mixture of water and oxygen gas (atoms are bonded), not a new element
checks.note: H2O2 decomposes into water and oxygen, but a liquid of H2O2 molecules is not that mixture.

checks.claim: Context: a compound holds its elements in fixed proportions (law of definite proportions)
John Dalton, an English chemist, set out his atomic theory in A New System of Chemical Philosophy, 1808
checks.note: 'Fully articulated in the first volume of A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808)'; first presented in a lecture in 1803.

checks.claim: Key: by Dalton's theory atoms of one element are all alike, with the same weight
checks.note: Atoms of one element 'identical in mass and properties'; different elements differ. True of real gold too: one stable isotope, 197Au (Grokipedia Gold).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: several kinds mixed / same atoms as every metal are contrary to Dalton's theory
Wrong choice: atoms are not each yellow and shiny; a single atom lacks the bulk material's colour and shine
checks.note: RSC: 'individual copper atoms have no colour', a misconception that 'atoms share the properties of the bulk material'.

checks.claim: Context: the alchemists before Dalton thought metals formed in the earth from sulfur and mercury
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'metals form in the earth through the mixing of sulfur and mercury', 'the basis of all theories of metallic composition until the 18th century'. Grokipedia (Alchemy) says only that Jabir 'treated metals as composites of intrinsic principles'; second confirmation from Albertus Magnus quoted in search results and the Ambix (Newman 2014) summary. Later alchemists added salt as a third principle (Paracelsus), so 'every metal from sulfur and mercury' is the dominant medieval view, fine as stated.

unit_notes: 11 questions: 9 ok, 1 error (3d82adc29a, one word), 1 uncertain (41bf99e830, minor wording). Alchemy (sulfur-mercury theory) confirmed on Wikipedia's Jabir page; Grokipedia's Alchemy page is thin on it and has no sulfur-mercury page, so secondary confirmation came from academic summaries in search results. Formulas and atom counts (NH3, Co vs CO/CO2, C6H12O6, SiO2 as a network ratio, O2/O3 allotropes, NaCl, NaOCl, NaOH, HCl, H2O2) all verified.
